extracted.intended_audience: political reformers, constitutional designers, legislators, and educated readers interested in institutional design of elective governments
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance and evaluative criteria for designing and judging elective institutions (legislatures, executives, upper chambers, elections) to secure stability, deliberation, and minimize party corruption. Focuses on mechanics like mode of election, composition, staggered terms, and anti-corruption safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent parliamentary anarchy / secure sufficient governing basis
rubrics_metrics.description: Parliamentary anarchy results when parties multiply and no party holds a sufficient basis; the system must avoid fragmentation that leaves government without sufficient support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay cites France, Italy, and Germany as examples where multiplicity of fractions has rendered ministries rickety and short-lived. Institutional design should aim to preserve a sufficiently broad foundation so governments are stable and able to act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit party dominance over conscience and public good
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid a system in which party allegiance is 'in fact higher than that which he owes to his political conscience or to the state.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Party discipline often forces sacrifice of conscience and freedom of opinion; legislation may be governed by party exigencies rather than the public good. Designs should reduce incentives and mechanisms that make party loyalty override public-spirited decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize corruption and bribery as instruments of organization
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize and reduce the near-inevitable use of bribery (money, patronage, titles, social grade) within party organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where tenure of office is secured by law (e.g., fixed terms), the need for bribery and patronage diminishes. The text recommends stamping political corruption as a crime and creating tribunals free from partisan influence for trying political offenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor statesmanship and deliberation over stump-oratory and demagoguery
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions should not reward mere 'stump-oratory' or charismatic tactics that fill imaginations but provide poor leadership; they should encourage deep statesmanship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because enfranchised masses may care little about 'great questions', institutional arrangements must promote thoughtful legislative work over continual electoral theatrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elect executive by the legislature (legislative election of executive council)
rubrics_metrics.description: The regular election of the Executive Council by members of the Legislature is proposed as the elective counterpart of a Privy Council and as a way to stabilize the executive while freeing both branches to perform proper functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benefits include renewal by installments to keep harmony, stable administration without fear for office existence, and removal of need for bribery used to hold followings together. Examples include Switzerland and virtually the English ministry designation by Commons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Renew executive and legislature by installments (staggered terms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Renewal by installments (staggered terms) keeps bodies in sufficient harmony with ongoing opinion and prevents disruptive cataclysms caused by general elections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Staggering allows steady inflow of public opinion, prevents ministerial dissolution abuse, and avoids general elections decided by single agitations. It is recommended for both executive councils and central legislatures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose ministers for departmental aptitude, not party patronage
rubrics_metrics.description: Ministers should be selected with regard to their administrative and departmental aptitudes instead of being appointed to satisfy party leaders and accommodate leaders with places.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This avoids the 'pitchforking system' where political considerations force placing party leaders into unsuitable departments and preserves quality administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define and secure a genuinely distinct role for an upper chamber
rubrics_metrics.description: A second chamber (Senate/Upper Chamber) must have a clear, distinct character and purpose; mere imitation of the House of Lords or a nominated body is inadequate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The House of Lords historically acted as a privileged order protecting its own interests; modern constitutions must specify what special elements the Upper Chamber is to consist of (age, wealth, wisdom) and weigh tradeoffs: age (weakness), wealth (odious), or wisdom (risk of being overridden by popular house).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid an appointed (nominated) senate controlled by the executive
rubrics_metrics.description: A Senate nominated by the Executive is an outrage on elective principle and in practice a 'nullity' prone to misuse as partisan tool.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Canadian example shows nominated Senates become infirmaries for partisans and can be abused under fierce partisan politics (e.g., used to force dissolutions). Prefer election or other mechanisms that confer independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not mechanically divide the national will between two independent organs
rubrics_metrics.description: Dividing the national will into two independent, co-equal organs (e.g., two elective chambers) tends toward collision and political convulsions rather than calm legislative review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experience (Victoria, France) shows collisions escalate into coercive dissolutions or revolts. Mechanical checks-and-balances inherited from times of monarchical jealousy are unsound for modern national unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secure deliberate legislative action by wise membership and procedural forms
rubrics_metrics.description: To ensure deliberation, assemblies should include the wisest men available and use legislative forms (e.g., suspensive vetoes, delays) to prevent haste and provide time for reflection and change of mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possible expedients include conferring a short suspensive veto on a stated minority and arranging forms of legislation that allow reflection; the aim is to secure deliberate action without provoking institutional collision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer a titular chief of state or collegial executive over a powerful elective president
rubrics_metrics.description: Elective presidencies with personal power are 'an almost unmixed evil'—they multiply patronage, elections, contests, disputed successions, and incentives to encroachment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay suggests a titular President of an Executive Council, or a collegial executive, with temporary powers in crises (akin to Roman dictatorship), to avoid the turmoil of elective personal chiefs. Historical examples: US presidency disputes (Hayes-Tilden) and Lincoln's wartime exception are discussed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor indirect election of central legislature (by local assemblies) over direct mass election
rubrics_metrics.description: Indirect election (members chosen by local assemblies) is preferable because nomination—the critical first step—is better performed by smaller, local bodies than by mass electorates where party machines usurp nominations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct election fails largely at the nomination stage: party caucuses and wire-pullers usurp nominations, leaving voters only a choice between party-set candidates. Indirect election elevates average ability (example: US Senate elected by state legislatures) and reduces party interference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design nomination mechanisms to prevent caucus/wire-puller domination
rubrics_metrics.description: Because nominations often determine elections, institutional arrangements must prevent usurpation of nominations by party organizations, caucuses, and wire-pullers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local assemblies and standing bodies of electors, operating under the eyes of their community, are less likely to be captured; temporary single-term colleges (like US Presidential electors) become nullities and should be avoided for sustained candidate selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strengthen and rely on local institutions as training schools for self-government
rubrics_metrics.description: Local institutions should be the basis of the system because they train citizens in self-government and produce better local candidates and electors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local elections with smaller areas have yielded good results (Canada example). Raising the importance of local assemblies will attract better men to public life, especially in cities, and reduce party interference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use standing assemblies of primary electors rather than temporary elector colleges
rubrics_metrics.description: A standing assembly of electors, periodically choosing members of higher legislatures, will be more effective than temporary election colleges created only for single terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A standing body provides continuity and informed selection (contrast with US presidential electors which can be a nullity or a mandate). The Senate elected by state legislatures is cited as an example of higher average ability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abolish or restrict ministerial power to dissolve the legislature
rubrics_metrics.description: End the 'ministerial prerogative of dissolution' by fixing legislative terms so ministers cannot dissolve parliament opportunistically to perpetuate power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fixed terms reduce the abuse where ministers dissolve when likely to win, thereby manipulating their tenure and creating instability. This supports the installment-renewal model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide impartial tribunals for political offenses and contested elections
rubrics_metrics.description: Political corruption and contested electoral matters should be adjudicated by tribunals free from partisan influence, rather than by parliamentary investigation or obsolete impeachment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parliamentary investigations under party systems become faction fights; a regular judicial or impartial tribunal with safeguards against malice should receive charges against public trust-holders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize and limit unavoidable human vices but design to reduce their sway
rubrics_metrics.description: Accept that vanity, intrigue, pique, self-interest, corruption, and narrowness cannot be entirely excluded, but arrange institutions so these bad influences are less determinative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For example, primary electors acting under community eyes are less likely to take direct bribes; tenure by law and institutional checks can diminish the inseparable sway of evil motives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure elections and institutions do not unnecessarily disrupt public life
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid institutional designs (e.g., long, frequent, or polarized presidential contests) that produce prolonged turmoil and disturb commercial/industrial life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elective presidencies and extended election cycles breed 'swarms of wire-pullers' and political vermin and keep party passions at fever-heat; staggered elections and less personalized executive selection reduce such disruption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use caution when transplanting British constitutional forms without the underlying realities
rubrics_metrics.description: Written constitutions that imitate the British form often copy forms but not the political realities (traditions, balances) and therefore misplace the stress of struggle (e.g., leaving power with the Crown in practice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When adopting features like a second chamber or ministerial appointment by the Crown, designers must consider local conditions and not assume British practices or traditions will carry over intact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider suspensive minority veto as an alternative to monarchic veto or bicameral collision
rubrics_metrics.description: A suspensive veto for a stated minority over a short period could be more effective than the obsolete Crown veto and less disruptive than bicameral collisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such an expedient would allow delay and reflection without provoking coercive dissolutions or swamping creations of peers; it is offered as a practical method to secure deliberate action.
